arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Welcome to this briefing on global CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and industry. We will trace emissions from the Industrial Revolution through 2024, drawing on the Global Carbon Budget 2025 dataset published via Our World in Data. [Pause]

Our focus: who emits, how much, and what's changing — the data behind the climate responsibility debate.

Key points: ① Scope covers fossil fuels and industry, 1750–2024 ② Data source: Global Carbon Budget 2025 ③ Audience: policy analysts, climate negotiators, sustainability researchers
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_emissions_growth

[Transition] Let's start with the big picture — the long-run trajectory of global CO₂ emissions.

In 1950, the world emitted roughly 6 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year. By 1990, that had more than tripled to over 20 billion tonnes. Today, we exceed 35 billion tonnes annually. [Data] That's nearly a sixfold increase in just 74 years. [Pause]

The critical point: while growth has slowed in recent years, global emissions have not yet peaked. We are still climbing.

Key points: ① 6 Bt in 1950 → >35 Bt in 2024 ② Post-1950 acceleration was the defining inflection ③ No peak yet despite slowing growth
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_regional_share_shift

[Transition] But who is responsible for these emissions? The answer has changed dramatically over time.

In 1900, Europe and the United States accounted for more than 90% of global CO₂ emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. Today, they account for less than one-third. [Pause]

The shift is striking: Asia, led by China, now produces roughly half of all global emissions. This is a fundamental transformation in the geography of carbon output.

Key points: ① Europe + US: >90% in 1900 → <33% today ② Asia now dominates, producing ~50% ③ Shift accelerated after 1970
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_china_dominates

[Transition] Within that Asian rise, one country stands out above all others.

China alone now emits approximately 31% of global CO₂ — more than the United States and the European Union combined. The US follows at roughly 13%, India at 8%, and the EU-27 at about 6%. [Pause]

Note that the entire continent of Africa accounts for only 3 to 4% of global emissions — comparable to international aviation and shipping.

Key points: ① China ~31%, US ~13%, India ~8%, EU ~6% ② China > US + EU combined ③ Africa's 1.4 billion people emit only 3–4% of global total
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_per_capita_inequality

[Transition] But total emissions tell only part of the story. Per capita figures reframe the question of responsibility entirely.

The average American or Canadian emits approximately 14 tonnes of CO₂ per year. The average person in Chad emits just 0.1 tonnes — a 150-fold difference. [Data] Put another way, an American emits in under two days what a Chadian emits in an entire year. [Pause]

The world average sits at about 4.5 tonnes per person. Most of Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia fall far below this line.

Key points: ① 150× gap between highest and lowest ② US/Canada ~14 t vs Chad ~0.1 t ③ World average ~4.5 t/person
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_per_capita_snapshot

[Transition] Let's look more closely at the per capita picture across major countries.

China may be the world's largest total emitter, but its per capita rate of about 9 tonnes is still 36% below the US level. India, despite being the third largest total emitter, sits at only 2 tonnes per person — well below the world average. [Pause]

Even among wealthy nations, the UK emits roughly 4 tonnes per capita — less than a third of the US figure. Total emissions and per capita responsibility paint very different pictures.

Key points: ① China: largest total but below US per capita ② India: 3rd largest total but very low per capita ③ UK vs US shows wealthy nations are not equal
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_annual_change_2024

[Transition] What happened in 2024? The picture is mixed.

Many Western nations — including the US, the EU, and the UK — saw emissions decline, shown in blue. Meanwhile, Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations experienced increases. Some countries in Central Asia saw particularly large increases exceeding 10%. [Pause]

The net effect: increases in developing nations partially offset declines in the West. Global emissions continued to rise, albeit slowly.

Key points: ① US, EU, UK saw declines ② Central Asia saw >10% increases ③ Net global trajectory: still rising
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 08_energy_mix

[Transition] Why do some wealthy nations emit so much less than others? The answer lies in energy mix.

France and the UK have per capita emissions of roughly 4 tonnes — about a quarter of the US figure — despite similar levels of prosperity. The key difference is that a much higher share of their electricity comes from nuclear power and renewable sources rather than fossil fuels. [Pause]

This is the most actionable insight in this briefing: energy technology and policy choices can decouple prosperity from emissions. It has already been done.

Key points: ① Similar GDP, very different emissions ② Nuclear and renewables drive the difference ③ Decoupling prosperity from emissions is proven possible
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 09_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with five key takeaways.

First, global emissions exceed 35 billion tonnes per year and have not yet peaked. Second, China is the largest annual emitter, but its per capita rate remains well below the US. Third, historical responsibility is dominated by Europe and the United States. Fourth, per capita gaps of 150 times persist between the richest and poorest nations. And fifth, energy policy and technology choices can and do decouple prosperity from emissions. [Pause]

The bottom line: responsibility for climate change is shared, but it is profoundly unequal — in total emissions, in per capita terms, and in historical contribution.

Key points: ① No peak yet ② Total ≠ per capita responsibility ③ Historical vs current emitters differ ④ 150× per capita gap ⑤ Energy policy is the lever
Duration: 1.5 minutes
